title: Northward trend signs survived one catch loss per year in two Northeast US trawl periods within 1982-2019
abstract: We tested the effect of lost catch from one shared haul per survey year on mean latitude trends. We used fixed strata and taxon cohorts in two US trawl surveys in 1982-2000 and 2001-2019. Effort counts stayed fixed, and each taxon had to retain positive catch. Both Northeast US fall trends stayed northward even when a loss was allowed in every year. Their exact bounds were +6.02 to +16.29 and +11.48 to +22.73 km per decade. Bering Sea trend signs could reverse with losses in at least 5 early-period years or 14 later-period years. A single affected year could not reverse any of the four signs. We give sharp budget bounds, an independent calculation check and source retrieval code. These are fixed-table sensitivity bounds, not confidence intervals. Survey bias, catchability, selected taxa and other error types remain outside the test. No climate or pollution cause was measured.

display.caption: Sharp trend bounds under admissible catch loss in at most k separate years. One shared haul can lose its catch in each affected year. Effort and taxon cohorts stay fixed. These are sensitivity bounds, not confidence intervals.

citations.reason: Verified published code informed fixed strata, cohort and cleaning rules. Raw data overlap; the new outcome is a shared-haul catch-loss bound.
Prior catch-quantile study in the same archive. Our test concerns haul influence on mean latitude trends.
